Being thus built by virtue of the promise of God, <hi type="italic">it shall not be plucked up, nor thrown down, any more for ever;</hi> that is, it shall continue very long, the time of the new city from the return to its last destruction being fully as long as that of the old from David to the captivity. But this promise was to have its full accomplishment in the gospel church, which, as it is the spiritual Israel, and therefore God will not cast it off, so it is the holy city, and therefore all the powers of men <hi type="italic">shall not pluck it up, nor throw it down.</hi> It may lie waste for a time, as Jerusalem did, but shall recover itself, shall weather the storm and gain its point, <hi type="italic">and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.31"/> <div eID="gen17897" type="x-p"/>

entries.20868fe9c57593292839935edf472d5860c7b20f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10251"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.31.1-Jer.31.40">Jr 31:1-40</reference>. Continuation of the Prophecy in the Thirtieth Chapter.</title> <div sID="gen18281" type="x-p"/> As in that chapter the restoration of Judah, so in this the restoration of Israel's ten tribes is foretold.<div eID="gen18281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18282" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10251"/><hi type="bold">1. At the same time--</hi>"In the latter days" (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.24">Jr 30:24</reference>).<div eID="gen18282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the God of--</hi>manifesting My grace to (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Ge 17:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.32">Mt 22:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>).<div eID="gen18283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... Israel--</hi>not the exiles of the south kingdom of Judah only, but also the north kingdom of the ten tribes; and not merely Israel in general, but "all the families of Israel." Never yet fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>). <div eID="gen18284" type="x-p"/>
entries.4eb5d1e86d9c489eee93293b86ab5bc9efa684dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10252"/><div sID="gen18285" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10252"/>2. Upon the grace manifested to Israel "in the wilderness" God grounds His argument for renewing His favors to them now in their exile; because His covenant is "everlasting" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jr 31:3</reference>), and changes not. The same argument occurs in <reference osisRef="Hos.13.5">Ho 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.4">14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.8">5, 8</reference>. Babylon is fitly compared to the "wilderness," as in both alike Israel was as a stranger far from his appointed "rest" or home, and Babylon is in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Is 40:3</reference> called a "desert" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jr 50:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I went to cause him to rest--</hi>namely, in the pillar of cloud and fire, the symbol of God's presence, which went before Israel to search a resting-place (<reference osisRef="Num.10.33">Nu 10:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.14">Is 63:14</reference>) for the people, both a temporary one at each halt in the wilderness, and a permanent one in Canaan (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.14">Ex 33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.20">De 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.44">Jos 21:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.95.11">Psa 95:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.11">He 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18286" type="x-p"/>
entries.f92354c84d7ce43496f5cebf5356067349e17e73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10253"/><div sID="gen18287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10253"/>3. Israel gratefully acknowledges in reply God's past grace; but at the same time tacitly implies by the expression "of old," that God does not appear to her now. "God appeared to me of old, but now I am forsaken!" God replies, Nay, I love thee with the same love now as of old. My love was not a momentary impulse, but from "everlasting" in My counsels, and to "everlasting" in its continuance; hence originated the covenant whereby I gratuitously adopted thee (Mal 1:2; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Ro 11:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.29">29</reference>). Margin translates, "from afar," which does not answer so well as "of old," to "in the wilderness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.2">Jr 31:2</reference>), which refers to the olden times of Israel's history.<div eID="gen18287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with loving kindness ... drawn--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Ho 11:4</reference>). Rather, "I have drawn out continually My loving kindness toward thee." So <reference osisRef="Ps.36.10">Psa 36:10</reference>, "Continue (Margin, 'Draw out at length') Thy loving kindness." By virtue of My everlasting love I will still extend My loving kindness to thee. So <reference osisRef="Isa.44.21">Is 44:21</reference>, "O Israel, thou shalt not be forgotten of Me." <div eID="gen18288" type="x-p"/>
entries.eba3b5b942b7106d8e82e6e1f659807eecf98026: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10254"/><div sID="gen18289" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10254"/><hi type="bold">4. I will build ... thou shalt be built--</hi>The combination of the active and passive to express the same fact implies the infallible certainty of its accomplishment. "Build," that is, establish in prosperity (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.7">Jr 33:7</reference>).<div eID="gen18289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adorned with ... tabrets--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference>). Or, "adorn thyself with thy timbrels"; used by damsels on occasions of public rejoicings (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Ex 15:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.11.34">Jud 11:34</reference>). Israel had cast away all instruments of joy in her exile (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.4">Psa 137:4</reference>).<div eID="gen18290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dances--</hi>holy joy, not carnal mirth. <div eID="gen18291" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9e92f21ceafdabf9e621145d430aa8242581fa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10255"/><div sID="gen18292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10255"/><hi type="bold">5. Samaria--</hi>the metropolis of the ten tribes; here equivalent to Israel. The mountainous nature of their country suited the growth of the vine.<div eID="gen18292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat ... as common--</hi>literally, "shall profane," that is, shall put to common use. For the first three years after planting, the vine was "not to be eaten of"; on the fourth year the fruit was to be "holy to praise the Lord withal"; on the fifth year the fruit was to be eaten as common, no longer restricted to holy use (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.23-Lev.19.25">Le 19:23-25</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.20.6">De 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">28:30</reference>, Margin). Thus the idea here is, "The same persons who plant shall reap the fruits"; it shall no longer be that one shall plant and another reap the fruit. <div eID="gen18293" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffad452c533fab7540cb1bb7e311cffd61433d6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10256"/><div sID="gen18294" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10256"/>6. The watchmen stationed on eminences (types of the preachers of the gospel), shall summon the ten tribes to go up to the annual feasts at Jerusalem ("Zion"), as they used to do before the revolt and the setting up of the idol calves at Dan and Beer-sheba (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.21">Eze 37:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen18294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Mount Ephraim--</hi>not one single mountain, but the whole mountainous region of the ten tribes.<div eID="gen18295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our God--</hi>from whom we formerly revolted, but who is now our God. An earnest of that good time to come is given in the partial success of the gospel in its first preaching in Samaria (<reference osisRef="John.4.1-John.4.42">Joh 4:1-42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.5-Acts.8.25">Ac 8:5-25</reference>). <div eID="gen18296" type="x-p"/>
entries.fabbe534256d3c240e7ae4571361018621d359fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10257"/><div sID="gen18297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10257"/>7. The people are urged with praises and prayers to supplicate for their universal restoration. Jehovah is represented in the context (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.1">Jr 31:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.8">8</reference>), as promising immediately to restore Israel. They therefore praise God for the restoration, being as certain of it as if it were actually accomplished; and at the same time pray for it, as prayer was a means to the desired end. Prayer does not move God to grant our wishes, but when God has determined to grant our wishes, He puts it into our hearts to pray for the thing desired. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.17">Psa 102:13-17</reference>, as to the connection of Israel's restoration with the prayers of His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.1-Isa.62.6">Is 62:1-6</reference>).<div eID="gen18297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for Jacob--</hi>on account of Jacob; on account of his approaching deliverance by Jehovah.<div eID="gen18298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among--</hi>"for," that is, on account of, would more exactly suit the parallelism to "for Jacob."<div eID="gen18299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief of the nations--</hi>Israel: as the parallelism to "Jacob" proves (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.4">Psa 135:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>). God estimates the greatness of nations not by man's standard of material resources, but by His electing favor. <div eID="gen18300" type="x-p"/>
entries.df6d36e3de4dfe55608de01a8930b30bad9db555: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10258"/><div sID="gen18301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10258"/><hi type="bold">8. north--</hi>Assyria, Media, &c. (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jr 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jr 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">23:8</reference>).<div eID="gen18301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather from ... coasts of ... earth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.34">Eze 20:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.41">41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.13">34:13</reference>).<div eID="gen18302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blind ... lame, &c.--</hi>Not even the most infirm and unfit persons for a journey shall be left behind, so universal shall be the restoration.<div eID="gen18303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a great company--</hi>or, they shall return "in a great company" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen18304" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c42c47f0583363417920f6dfaa996e4756ec56a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10259"/><div sID="gen18305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10259"/><hi type="bold">9. weeping--</hi>for their past sins which caused their exile (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.5">Psa 126:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.6">6</reference>). Although they come with weeping, they shall return with joy (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.4">Jr 50:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen18305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">supplications--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jr 31:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.21-Jer.3.25">Jr 3:21-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>). Margin translates "favors," as in <reference osisRef="Josh.11.20">Jos 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezr 9:8</reference>; thus God's favors or compassions are put in opposition to the people's weeping; their tears shall be turned into joy. But English Version suits the parellelism best.<div eID="gen18306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will cause ... to walk by ... waters ... straight way--</hi>(Is 35:6-8; 43:<reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.10">49:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.11">11</reference>). God will give them waters to satisfy their thirst as in the wilderness journey from Egypt. So spiritually (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">Mt 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>).<div eID="gen18307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ephraim--</hi>the ten tribes no longer severed from Judah, but forming one people with it.<div eID="gen18308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my first-born--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Ex 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>). So the elect Church (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.18">2Co 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>). <div eID="gen18309" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ffcb3b98851f8a86727a8d36490b580e8937870: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10260"/><div sID="gen18310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10260"/>10. The tidings of God's interposition in behalf of Israel will arrest the attention of even the uttermost Gentile nations.<div eID="gen18310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He that scattered will gather--</hi>He who scattered knows where to find Israel; He who smote can also heal.<div eID="gen18311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep--</hi>not only will gather, but keep safely to the end (<reference osisRef="John.13.1">Joh 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.11">17:11</reference>).<div eID="gen18312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shepherd--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Is 40:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12-Ezek.34.14">Eze 34:12-14</reference>). <div eID="gen18313" type="x-p"/>
entries.48c93125d97121f2592ce7ad337d9cad329bb64c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10261"/><div sID="gen18314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10261"/><hi type="bold">11. ransomed ... from ... hand of ... stronger--</hi>No strength of the foe can prevent the Lord from delivering Jacob (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.24">Is 49:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.25">25</reference>). <div eID="gen18314" type="x-p"/>
entries.07a89270739b082a096294a6921a22665ffe6541: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10262"/><div sID="gen18315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10262"/><hi type="bold">12. height of Zion--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>).<div eID="gen18315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flow--</hi>There shall be a conflux of worshippers to the temple on Zion (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mi 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen18316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the goodness of ... Lord--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Jer.31.14">Jr 31:14</reference>). Beneficence, that is, to the Lord as the source of all good things (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>), to pray to Him and praise Him for these blessings of which He is the Fountainhead.<div eID="gen18317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watered garden--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Is 58:11</reference>). Not merely for a time, but continually full of holy comfort.<div eID="gen18318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not sorrow any more--</hi>referring to the Church triumphant, as well as to literal Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Is 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.19">65:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Re 21:4</reference>). <div eID="gen18319" type="x-p"/>
entries.e20221067a367f57e806085901d57024bfd3b85e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10263"/><div sID="gen18320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10263"/><hi type="bold">13. young ... old--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.8.4">Zec 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen18320" type="x-p"/>
entries.631f051cc9cc1dc297e29d098a3b2063035680ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10264"/><div sID="gen18321" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10264"/><hi type="bold">14. my goodness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jr 31:12</reference>). <div eID="gen18321" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c77e916c33345a3dc3ba933a3645863fa08e0f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10265"/><div sID="gen18322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10265"/><hi type="bold">15. Ramah--</hi>In Benjamin, east of the great northern road, two hours' <hi type="bold">journey from Jerusalem. Rachel, who all her life had pined for children (<reference osisRef="Gen.30.1">Ge 30:1</reference>), and who died with "sorrow" in giving birth to Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.18">Ge 35:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.19">19</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>), and was buried at Ramah, near Beth-lehem, is represented as raising her head from the tomb, and as breaking forth into "weeping" at seeing the whole land depopulated of her sons, the Ephraimites. Ramah was the place where Nebuzara-dan collected all the Jews in chains, previous to their removal to Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.1">Jr 40:1</reference>). God therefore consoles her with the promise of their restoration. <reference osisRef="Matt.2.17">Mt 2:17</reference>, 18 quotes this as fulfilled in the massacre of the innocents under Herod. "A lesser and a greater event, of different times, may answer to the single sense of one passage of Scripture, until the prophecy is exhausted" [Bengel]. Besides the temporary reference to the exiles in Babylon, the Holy Spirit foreshadowed ultimately Messiah's exile in Egypt, and the desolation caused in the neighborhood of Rachel's tomb by Herod's massacre of the children, whose mothers had "sons of sorrow" (Ben-oni), just as Rachel had. The return of Messiah (the representative of Israel) from Egypt, and the future restoration of Israel, both the literal and the spiritual (including the innocents), at the Lord's second advent, are antitypical of the restoration of Israel from Babylon, which is the ground of consolation held out here by Jeremiah. The clause, "They were not," that is, were dead (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.13">Ge 42:13</reference>), does not apply so strictly to the exiles in Babylon as it does to the history of Messiah and His people--</hi>past, present, and future. So the words, "There is hope in thine end," are to be fulfilled ultimately, when Rachel shall meet her murdered children at the resurrection, at the same time that literal Israel is to be restored. "They were not," in Hebrew, is singular; each was not: each mother at the Beth-lehem massacre had but one child to lament, as the limitation of age in Herod's order, "two years and under," implies; this use of the singular distributively (the mothers weeping severally, each for her own child), is a coincidence between the prophecy of the Beth-lehem massacre and the event, the more remarkable as not being obvious: the singular, too, is appropriate as to Messiah in His Egyptian exile, who was to be a leading object of Rachel's lamentation. <div eID="gen18322" type="x-p"/>
entries.298f7af066ccafdcca54ab65483c2973410a2635: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10266"/><div sID="gen18323" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10266"/><hi type="bold">16. thy work--</hi>thy parental weeping for thy children [Rosenmuller]. Thine affliction in the loss of thy children, murdered for Christ's sake, shall not be fruitless to thee, as was the case in thy giving birth to the "child of thy sorrow," Benjamin. Primarily, also, thy grief shall not be perpetual: the exiles shall return, and the land be inhabited again [Calvin].<div eID="gen18323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come again--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18324" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2069eda488b8fc313afc817cdee53ee91ba19c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10267"/><div sID="gen18325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10267"/><hi type="bold">17. hope in ... end--</hi>All thy calamities shall have a prosperous issue. <div eID="gen18325" type="x-p"/>
entries.b432d96e19512ad0e40c3304e2cbc7789c25b749: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10268"/><div sID="gen18326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10268"/><hi type="bold">18. Ephraim--</hi>representing the ten tribes.<div eID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bemoaning himself--</hi>The spirit of penitent supplication shall at last be poured on Israel as the necessary forerunner of their restoration (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.14">Zec 12:10-14</reference>).<div eID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised--</hi>In the first clause the chastisement itself is meant; in the second the beneficial effect of it in teaching the penitent true wisdom.<div eID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bullock unaccustomed to ... yoke--</hi>A similar image occurs in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>. Compare "stiff-necked," <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.9">Ex 32:9</reference>, an image from refractory oxen. Before my chastisement I needed the severe correction I received, as much as an untamed bullock needs the goad. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.9.5">Ac 9:5</reference>, where the same figure is used of Saul while unconverted. Israel has had a longer chastisement than Judah, not having been restored even at the Jews' return from Babylon. Hereafter, at its restoration, it shall confess the sore discipline was all needed to "accustom" it to God's "easy yoke" (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">30</reference>).<div eID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn thou me--</hi>by Thy converting Spirit (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.21">La 5:21</reference>). But why does Ephraim pray for conversion, seeing that he is already converted? Because we are converted by progressive steps, and need the same power of God to carry forward, as to originate, our conversion (<reference osisRef="John.6.44">Joh 6:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.65">65</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Is 27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1Pe 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18330" type="x-p"/>
entries.803bc1c5487d8c8a420eceb128c34846bca7a436: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10269"/><div sID="gen18331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10269"/><hi type="bold">19. after that I was turned, I repented--</hi>Repentance in the full sense follows, not precedes, our being turned to God by God (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>). The Jews' "looking to Him whom they pierced" shall result in their "mourning for Him." Repentance is the tear that flows from the eye of faith turned to Jesus. He Himself gives it: we give it not of ourselves, but must come to Him for it (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.31">Ac 5:31</reference>).<div eID="gen18331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">instructed--</hi>made to learn by chastisement. God's Spirit often works through the corrections of His providence.<div eID="gen18332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smote upon ... thigh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.12">Eze 21:12</reference>). A token of indignant remorse, shame, and grief, because of his past sin.<div eID="gen18333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bear ... reproach of ... youth--</hi>"because the calamities which I bore were the just punishment of my scandalous wantonness against God in my youth"; alluding to the idols set up at Dan and Beth-el immediately after the ten tribes revolted from Judah. His sense of shame shows that he no longer delights in his sin. <div eID="gen18334" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cbc71803ae86971a8c9be37dbef7425e10cac33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10270"/><div sID="gen18335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10270"/><hi type="bold">20. Is Ephraim my dear son? &c.--</hi>The question implies that a negative answer was to be expected. Who would have thought that one so undutiful to His heavenly Father as Ephraim had been should still be regarded by God as a "pleasant child?" Certainly he was not so in respect to his sin. But by virtue of God's "everlasting love" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jr 31:3</reference>) on Ephraim's being "turned" to God, he was immediately welcomed as God's "dear son." This verse sets forth God's readiness to welcome the penitent (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jr 31:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.19">19</reference>), anticipating his return with prevenient grace and love. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.15.20">Lu 15:20</reference>: "When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion," &c.<div eID="gen18335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spake against--</hi>threatened him for his idolatry.<div eID="gen18336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember--</hi>with favor and concern, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.8.1">Ge 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.30.22">30:22</reference>.<div eID="gen18337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bowels ... troubled for him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">De 32:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Is 63:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8">Ho 11:8</reference>)--namely, with the yearnings of compassionate love. The "bowels" include the region of the heart, the seat of the affections. <div eID="gen18338" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fafaefaac54e3343b6bbd40570b586865fa53f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10271"/><div sID="gen18339" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10271"/><hi type="bold">21. waymarks--</hi>pillars to mark the road for the returning exiles. Caravans set up pillars, or pointed heaps of stones, to mark the way through the desert against their return. So Israel is told by God to mark the way by which they went in leaving their country for exile; for by the same way they shall return.<div eID="gen18339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">highway--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Is 35:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen18340" type="x-p"/>
entries.8aa95fac5250c02b33bc3a991c9140868b531ee1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10272"/><div sID="gen18341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10272"/><hi type="bold">22. go about--</hi>namely, after human helps (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jr 2:18</reference>, 23, 36). Why not return immediately to me? Maurer translates, as in <reference osisRef="Song.5.6">So 5:6</reference>, "How long wilt thou withdraw thyself?" Let thy past backslidings suffice thee now that a new era approaches. What God finds fault with in them is, that they looked hither and thither, leaning on contingencies, instead of at once trusting the word of God, which promised their restoration. To assure them of this, God promises to create a new thing in their land, A woman shall compass a man. Calvin explains this: Israel, who is feeble as a woman, shall be superior to the warlike Chaldeans; the captives shall reduce their captors to captivity. Hengstenberg makes the "woman" the Jewish Church, and the "man" Jehovah, her husband, whose love she will again seek (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.6">Ho 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>). Maurer, A woman shall protect (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">De 32:10</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">Psa 32:10</reference>) a man, that is, You need fear no foes in returning, for all things shall be so peaceful that a woman would be able to take man's part, and act as his protector. But the Christian fathers (Augustine, &c.) almost unanimously interpreted it of the Virgin Mary compassing Christ in her womb. This view is favored:--(1) By the connection; it gives a reason why the exiles should desire a return to their country, namely, because Christ was conceived there. (2) The word "created" implies a divine power put forth in the creation of a body in the Virgin's womb by the Holy Ghost for the second Adam, such as was exerted in creating the first Adam (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">Lu 1:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.3">3</reference>) The phrase, "a new thing," something unprecedented; a man whose like had never existed before, at once God and man; a mother out of the ordinary course of nature, at once mother and virgin. An extraordinary mode of generation; one conceived by the Holy Ghost without man. (4) The specification "in the land" (not "earth," as English Version), namely, of Judah, where probably Christ was conceived, in Hebron (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.39">Lu 1:39</reference>, 42, 44, with <reference osisRef="Josh.21.11">Jos 21:11</reference>) or else in Nazareth, "in the territory" of Israel, to whom <reference osisRef="Jer.31.5">Jr 31:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.15">6, 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.21">18, 21</reference> refer; His birth was at Beth-lehem (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mi 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.2.5">Mt 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">6</reference>). As the place of His nativity, and of His being reared (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.23">Mt 2:23</reference>), and of His preaching (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>; Mal 3:1), are specified, so it is likely the Holy Spirit designated the place of His being conceived. (5) The Hebrew for "woman" implies an individual, as the Virgin Mary, rather than a collection of persons. (6) The restoration of Israel is grounded on God's covenant in Christ, to whom, therefore, allusion is naturally made as the foundation of Israel's hope (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>). The Virgin Mary's conception of Messiah in the womb answers to the "Virgin of Israel" (therefore so called, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.21">Jr 31:21</reference>), that is, Israel and her sons at their final restoration, receiving Jesus as Messiah (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.7">7</reference>) The reference to the conception of the child Messiah accords with the mention of the massacre of "children" referred to in <reference osisRef="Jer.31.15">Jr 31:15</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.2.17">Mt 2:17</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>) The Hebrew for "man" is properly "mighty man," a term applied to God (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">De 10:17</reference>); and to Christ (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zec 13:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">Psa 45:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>) [Calovius]. <div eID="gen18341" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1f6c22e0e7c0e4abf5330185849203704384bb9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10273"/><div sID="gen18342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10273"/>23. Jerusalem again shall be the metropolis of the whole nation, the seat of "justice" (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.5-Ps.122.8">Psa 122:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Is 1:26</reference>), and of sacred worship ("holiness," <reference osisRef="Zech.8.3">Zec 8:3</reference>) on "Mount" Moriah. <div eID="gen18342" type="x-p"/>
entries.492e149d26462cb98843242f0dc86993a8f971ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10274"/><div sID="gen18343" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10274"/><hi type="bold">24. Judah ... cities ... husbandmen ... they with flocks--</hi>Two classes, citizens and countrymen, the latter divided into agriculturists and shepherds, all alike in security, though the latter were to be outside the protection of city walls. "Judah" here stands for the country, as distinguished from its cities. <div eID="gen18343" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9c4610b571215785f94e26d79932b11f3e23867: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10275"/><div sID="gen18344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10275"/>25. The "weary, sorrowful," and indigent state of Israel will prove no obstacle in the way of My helping them. <div eID="gen18344" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbaf5308368ce54a5b50b70269e1c0a58393285b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10276"/><div sID="gen18345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10276"/>26. The words of Jeremiah: Upon this (or, By reason of this) announcement of a happy restoration, "I awaked" from the prophetic dream vouchsafed to me (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.25">Jr 23:25</reference>) with the "sweet" impression thereof remaining on my mind. "Sleep" here means dream, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>. <div eID="gen18345" type="x-p"/>
entries.acefe45c76a6ff462d4af82e78282e8d91a06c94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10277"/><div sID="gen18346" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10277"/>27. He shows how a land so depopulated shall again be peopled. God will cause both men and beasts in it to increase to a multitude (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.9-Ezek.36.11">Eze 36:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Ho 2:23</reference>). <div eID="gen18346" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0189e38c1f1b4a883f5a59e12acd2a8d4a77d87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10278"/><div sID="gen18347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10278"/>28. (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.27">Jr 44:27</reference>). The same God who, as it were (in human language), was on the watch for all means to destroy, shall be as much on the watch for the means of their restoration. <div eID="gen18347" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ecdfa4d9bfa0ca91253817a75fa7c668602abcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10279"/><div sID="gen18348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10279"/><hi type="bold">29. In those days--</hi>after their punishment has been completed, and mercy again visits them.<div eID="gen18348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fathers ... eaten ... sour grape ... children's teeth ... on edge--</hi>the proverb among the exiles' children born in Babylon, to express that they suffered the evil consequences of their fathers' sins rather than of their own (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.7">La 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.2">Eze 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen18349" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf55649afd39ddffe14eb3132ddd30b2cddce122: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10280"/><div sID="gen18350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10280"/>30. (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.5">Ga 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen18350" type="x-p"/>
entries.2904882908323d5401359c42d1d649d09902c24b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10281"/><div sID="gen18351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10281"/><hi type="bold">31. the days ... new covenant with ... Israel ... Judah--</hi>The new covenant is made with literal Israel and Judah, not with the spiritual Israel, that is, believers, except secondarily, and as grafted on the stock of Israel (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.16-Rom.11.27">Ro 11:16-27</reference>). For the whole subject of the thirtieth and thirty-first chapters is the restoration of the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.4">Jr 30:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">7, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.7">31:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">10, 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.24">23, 24</reference>, 27, 36). With the "remnant according to the election of grace" in Israel, the new covenant has already taken effect. But with regard to the whole nation, its realization is reserved for the last days, to which Paul refers this prophecy in an abridged form (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.27">Ro 11:27</reference>). <div eID="gen18351" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2413987858f528ba1335d52d3c6f0eb0a166b04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10282"/><div sID="gen18352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10282"/><hi type="bold">32. Not ... the covenant that I made with ... fathers--</hi>the Old Testament covenant, as contrasted with our gospel covenant (He 8:8-12; 10:16, 17, where this prophecy is quoted to prove the abrogation of the law by the gospel), of which the distinguishing features are its securing by an adequate atonement the forgiveness of sins, and by the inworking of effectual grace ensuring permanent obedience. An earnest of this is given partially in the present eclectic or elect Church gathered out of Jews and Gentiles. But the promise here to Israel in the last days is national and universal, and effected by an extraordinary outpouring of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.33">Jr 31:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.17-Ezek.11.20">Eze 11:17-20</reference>), independent of any merit on their part (Eze 36:25-32; 37:1-28; 39:29; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23-Joel.2.28">Joe 2:23-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.16">2Co 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen18352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">took ... by ... hand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">De 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.3">Ho 11:3</reference>).<div eID="gen18353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">although I was an husband--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.7">Ho 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). But the Septuagint, Syriac, and St. Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.9">He 8:9</reference>) translate, "I regarded them not"; and Gesenius, &c., justify this rendering of the Hebrew from the Arabic. The Hebrews regarded not God, so God regarded them not. <div eID="gen18354" type="x-p"/>
entries.dab4cf8cd4a8268f4900aa0c748230cab6cb0754: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10283"/><div sID="gen18355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10283"/><hi type="bold">33. will be their God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.32.38">Jr 32:38</reference>). <div eID="gen18355" type="x-p"/>
entries.d67d1931ec328f4d06a92f30f9f50c8dfac0e2d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10284"/><div sID="gen18356" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10284"/>34. True, specially of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Is 54:13</reference>); secondarily, true of believers (<reference osisRef="John.6.45">Joh 6:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen18356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgive ... iniquity ... remember ... no more--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.33.8">Jr 33:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.20">50:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>); applying peculiarly to Israel (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.27">Ro 11:27</reference>). Secondarily, all believers (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.43">Ac 10:43</reference>). <div eID="gen18357" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbdf563fa7ea77c3967c339a391dc93196f562ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10285"/><div sID="gen18358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10285"/><hi type="bold">35. divideth ... sea when ... waves ... roar ... Lord of hosts ... name--</hi>quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.51.15">Is 51:15</reference>, the genuineness of which passage is thus established on Jeremiah's authority. <div eID="gen18358" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b79bfd91ad222e1f33ca9bda07a6a3db805965b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10286"/><div sID="gen18359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10286"/><hi type="bold">36. a nation--</hi>Israel's national polity has been broken up by the Romans. But their preservation as a distinct people amidst violent persecutions, though scattered among all nations for eighteen centuries, unamalgamated, whereas all other peoples under such circumstances have become incorporated with the nations in which they have been dispersed, is a perpetual standing miracle (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.33.20">Jr 33:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.148.6">Psa 148:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Is 54:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen18359" type="x-p"/>
entries.58d524b8922a6f4445b3b33930c48225b716706b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10287"/><div sID="gen18360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10287"/>37. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.33.22">Jr 33:22</reference>).<div eID="gen18360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for all that they have done--</hi>namely, all the sins. God will regard His own covenant promise, rather than their merits. <div eID="gen18361" type="x-p"/>
entries.722b25126855335c86acd6429f751eb6b80ee47d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10288"/><div sID="gen18362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10288"/><hi type="bold">38. tower of Hananeel--</hi>The city shall extend beyond its former bounds (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Ne 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.39">12:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.10">Zec 14:10</reference>).<div eID="gen18362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gate of ... corner--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.13">2Ki 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.9">2Ch 26:9</reference>). <div eID="gen18363" type="x-p"/>
entries.064015ff5cb34c5d693a6aa915266fbcfe09b3d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10289"/><div sID="gen18364" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10289"/><hi type="bold">39. measuring-line--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.8">Eze 40:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.1">Zec 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen18364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gareb--</hi>from a Hebrew root, "to scrape"; Syriac, "leprosy"; the locality outside of the city, to which lepers were removed.<div eID="gen18365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Goath--</hi>from a root, "to toil," referring to the toilsome ascent there: outside of the city of David, towards the southwest, as Gareb was northwest [Junius]. <div eID="gen18366" type="x-p"/>
entries.ade83de3973f6f69550af800b815037bf07f5e7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10290"/><div sID="gen18367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10290"/><hi type="bold">40. valley of ... dead--</hi>Tophet, where the bodies of malefactors were cast (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>), south of the city.<div eID="gen18367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fields ... Kidron--</hi>so <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">2Ki 23:4</reference>. Fields in the suburbs reaching as far as Kidron, east of the city.<div eID="gen18368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horse gate--</hi>Through it the king's horses were led forth for watering to the brook Kidron (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.16">2Ki 11:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.28">Ne 3:28</reference>).<div eID="gen18369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>The city shall not only be spacious, but both "holy to the Lord," that is, freed from all pollutions, and everlasting (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.17">Joe 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>, 10, 27). <chapter eID="Jer.31"/>

entries.2b1f9b3c2ecf50e696e96dd6dcf52ae10fda45a2: <div eID="gen30112" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30113" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30114" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30114" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30113" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30115" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues the subject of the preceding in a beautiful vision represented at a distant period. God is introduced expressing his continual regard for Israel, and promising to restore them to their land and liberty, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.1-Jer.31.5">Jer 31:1-5</reference>. Immediately heralds appear, proclaiming on Mount Ephraim the arrival of the great year of jubilee, and summoning the people to gather unto Zion, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.6">Jer 31:6</reference>. Upon which God resumes the speech; and makes such gracious promises both of leading them tenderly by the way, and making them happy in their own land, that all the nations of the world are called upon to consider with deep attention this great salvation, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.7-Jer.31.14">Jer 31:7-14</reference>. The scene is then diversified by a very happy invention. Rachel, the another of Joseph and Benjamin, is represented as risen from her tomb, in a city of Benjamin near Jerusalem, looking about for her children, and bitterly lamenting their fate, as none of them are to be seen in the land of their fathers, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.15">Jer 31:15</reference>. But she is consoled with the assurance that they are not lost, and that they shall in due time be restored, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.16">Jer 31:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.17">Jer 31:17</reference>. To this another tender and beautiful scene immediately succeeds. Ephraim, (often put for the Ten tribes), comes in view. He laments his past errors, and expresses the most earnest desires of reconciliation; upon which God, as a tender parent, immediately forgives him, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18-Jer.31.20">Jer 31:18-20</reference>. The virgin of Israel is then directed to prepare for returning home, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.21">Jer 31:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.22">Jer 31:22</reference>; and the vision closes with a promise of abundant peace and security to Israel and Judah in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.23-Jer.31.26">Jer 31:23-26</reference>. The blessed condition of Israel under the Messiah's reign is then beautifully contrasted with their afflicted state during the general dispersion, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.27">Jer 31:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.28">Jer 31:28</reference>. In the remaining part of the chapter the promises to the posterity of Jacob of the impartial administration of justice, increasing peace and prosperity, the universal diffusion of righteousness, and stability in their own land after a general restoration in Gospel tines, are repeated, enlarged on, and illustrated by a variety of beautiful figures, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.29-Jer.31.40">Jer 31:29-40</reference>. <div eID="gen30115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30116" type="x-p"/> Dr. Blayney has introduced this and the preceding chapter with the following excellent observations: - "There are many prophecies," says he, "in various parts of the Old Testament, which announce the future restoration of Israel to their own land, and the complete re-establishment of both their civil and religious constitution in the latter days, meaning the times of the Gospel dispensation. These two chapters contain a prophecy of this kind; which must necessarily be referred to these times, because it points out circumstances which certainly were not fulfilled at the return of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, nor have hitherto had their completion. For the people who returned from Babylon were the people of Judah only, who had been carried away captive by Nebuchadnezzar; but here it is foretold, that not only should the captivity of Judah be restored, but the captivity of Israel also, meaning those ten tribes which were carried away before, by Shalmaneser king of Assyria; and who still remain in their several dispersions, having never returned, in a national capacity at least, to their own land, whatever some few individuals have done. But the terms of the prophecy entitle us to expect, not an obscure and partial, but a complete and universal, restoration; when God will manifest himself, as formerly, the God and Patron of all the families of Israel, and not of a few only. Again it is promised that, after this restoration, they should no more fall under the dominion of foreigners, but be governed by princes and magistrates of their own nation, independently of any but God, and David their king. But this was not the case with the Jews who returned from Babylon. They then indeed had a leader, Zerubbabel, one of their own nation, and also of the family of David; but both the nation and their leader continued still in a state of vassalage, and the most servile dependence upon the Persian monarchy. And when the Grecian monarchy succeeded, they changed their masters only, but not their condition; till at length under the Asmonean princes they had for a while an independent government of their own, but without any title to the name of David. At last they fell under the Roman yoke; since which time their situation has been such as not to afford the least ground to pretend that the promised restoration has yet taken place. It remains therefore to be brought about in future under the reign of the Messiah, emphatically distinguished by the name of David; when every particular circumstance predicted concerning it will no doubt be verified by a distinct and unequivocal accomplishment. There is no particular date annexed to this prophecy, whereby to ascertain the precise time of its delivery. But it may not unreasonably be presumed to have followed immediately after the preceding one in which the restoration of the people from their Babylonish captivity is in direct terms foretold. From hence the transition is natural and easy to the more glorious and general restoration which was to take place in a more distant period, and was designed for the ultimate object of the national hopes and expectations. Both events are frequently thus connected together in the prophetic writings; and perhaps with this design, that when that which was nearest at hand should be accomplished, it might afford the clearest, and strongest, and most satisfactory kind of evidence that the latter, how remote soever its period, would in like manner be brought about by the interposition of Providence in its due season. But though this prophecy relates wholly to one single subject, it seems naturally to divide itself into three distinct parts. <div eID="gen30116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30117" type="x-p"/> The first part, after a short preface, in which the prophet is required to commit to writing the matters revealed to him, commences with representing, in a style of awe and energy, the consternation and distress which, in some future day of visitation, should fall upon all nations, preparatory to the scene of Jacob's deliverance, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.5-Jer.30.9">Jer 30:5-9</reference>. Israel is encouraged to confide in the Divine assurance of restoration and protection, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">Jer 30:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jer 30:11</reference>. He is prepared previously to expect a severe chastisement for the multitude of his sins; but consoled with the prospect of a happy termination, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.12-Jer.30.17">Jer 30:12-17</reference>. This is followed by an enumeration at large of the blessings and privileges to which the Jews should be restored upon their re-admission into God's favor, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.18-Jer.30.22">Jer 30:18-22</reference>. Again, however, it is declared that the anger of Jehovah would not subside till his purposed vengeance against the wicked should have been fully executed; and then, but not till then, an entire reconciliation would take place between him and all the families of Israel, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.23">Jer 30:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.1">Jer 31:1</reference>. <div eID="gen30117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30118" type="x-p"/> The second part of this prophecy begins chap. <reference osisRef="Jer.31.2">Jer 31:2</reference>, and is marked by a sudden transition to a distant period of time, represented in a vision, and embellished with a variety of beautiful scenes and images. God announces the renewal of his ancient love for Israel; and promises, in consequence thereof, a speedy restoration of their former privileges and happiness, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.2-Jer.31.5">Jer 31:2-5</reference>. Already the heralds have proclaimed on Mount Ephraim the arrival of the joyful day; they summon the people to re-assemble once more in Zion; and promulge by special command the glad tidings of salvation which God had accomplished for them. God himself declares his readiness to conduct home the remnant of Israel from all parts of their dispersion, to compassionate and relieve their infirmities, and to provide them with all necessary accommodations by the way, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.6-Jer.31.9">Jer 31:6-9</reference>. The news is carried into distant lands; and the nations are summoned to attend to the display of God's power and goodness in rescuing his people from their stronger enemies, and in supplying them after their return with all manner of good things to the full extent of their wants and desires, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.10-Jer.31.14">Jer 31:10-14</reference>. Here the scene changes; and two new personages are successively introduced, in order to diversify the same subject, and to impress it more strongly. Rachel first; who is represented as just risen from the grave, and bitterly bewailing the loss of her children; for whom she anxiously looks about, but none are to be seen. Her tears are dried up; and she is consoled with the assurance that they are not lost for ever, but shall in time be brought back to their ancient borders, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.15-Jer.31.17">Jer 31:15-17</reference>. Ephraim comes next. He laments his past undutifulness with great contrition and penitence, and professes an earnest desire of amendment. These symptoms of returning duty are no sooner discerned in him, than God acknowledges him once more as a darling child and resolves with mercy to receive him, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18-Jer.31.20">Jer 31:18-20</reference>. The virgin of Israel is then earnestly exhorted to hasten the preparations for their return; and encouraged with having the prospect of a signal miracle wrought in her favor, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.21">Jer 31:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.22">Jer 31:22</reference>. And the vision closes at last with a promise that the Divine blessing should again rest upon the land of Judah; and that the men of Judah should once more dwell there, cultivating it according to the simplicity of ancient institutions, and fully discharged from every want, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.23-Jer.31.26">Jer 31:23-26</reference>. In the third part, by way of appendix to the vision, the following gracious promises are specifically annexed: That God would in time to come supply all the deficiencies of Israel and Judah; and would be as diligent to restore as he had ever been to destroy them; and would not any more visit the offenses of the fathers upon the children, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.27-Jer.31.30">Jer 31:27-30</reference>. That he would make with them a better covenant than he had made with their forefathers, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34">Jer 31:31-34</reference>. That they should continue his people by an ordinance as firm and as lasting as that of the heavens, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35-Jer.31.37">Jer 31:35-37</reference>. And that Jerusalem should again be built, enlarged in its extent, and secure from future desolation, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38-Jer.31.40">Jer 31:38-40</reference>." <div eID="gen30118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30119" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30120" type="x-p"/> At the same time - This discourse was delivered at the same time with the former; and, with that, constitutes the Book which God ordered the prophet to write. <div eID="gen30120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30121" type="x-p"/> Will I be the God of all the families of Israel - I shall bring back the ten tribes, as well as their brethren the Jews. The restoration of the Israelites is the principal subject of this chapter.
entries.f9f208e8fa07f954788e670409c8fe685178ea05: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30122" type="x-p"/> The people which were left of the sword - Those of the ten tribes that had escaped death by the sword of the Assyrians. <div eID="gen30122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30123" type="x-p"/> Found grace in the wilderness - The place of their exile; a wilderness, compared to their own land. - Dahler. See <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>
entries.9c4caa3b3ae6f2d1a895518787f997140ae85fc4: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30124" type="x-p"/> I have loved thee with an everlasting love - ואהבת עולם אהבתיך veahabath olam ahabtich, "and with the old love I have loved thee." "Also, with a love of long standing have I loved thee." - Blayney. "But I love thee always." - Dahler. I still bear to the Jewish people that love which I showed to their fathers in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in the promised land. Can it be supposed, by any person seriously considering the context, that these words are spoken of God's decree of election in behalf of the Jews? Those who make it such, act most injudiciously on their own principle; for, how few of the Jews have ever given evidence that they were the children of God, from their restoration from Babylon to the present day! The words refer simply to their state as a people, most wondrously preserved by the providence and mercy of God, as a standing proof of the Divine authority of the Scriptures, and as an evidence of God's displeasure against sin. <div eID="gen30124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30125" type="x-p"/> Therefore with loving-kindness have I drawn thee - "Therefore have I lengthened out mercy to thee." - Blayney, <div eID="gen30125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30126" type="x-p"/> C'est pourquoi je t'ai conserve ma grace. <div eID="gen30126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30127" type="x-p"/> Dahler. "Therefore I have preserved my grace to thee." <div eID="gen30127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30128" type="x-p"/> The exiles, who had not for a long time received any proofs of the Divine protection, are represented as deploring their state; but God answers, that though this may seem to be the case, he has always loved them; and this continued love he will show by bringing them out of their captivity. However creeds may fare, this is the sense of the passage; all the context proves this.
entries.7d04cd3b2cc25f8c310702f51b19dd8efc9f135f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30129" type="x-p"/> O virgin of Israel - Israelites in general; now called virgin, because restored to their ancient purity. <div eID="gen30129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30130" type="x-p"/> With thy tabrets - Women in general played on these; they were used in times of rejoicing, and accompanied with dancing. To these customs, still preserved, the prophet alludes.
entries.d2897f513ba7821d98c987d55183c60a5816223a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30131" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria - This was the regal city of the Israelites, as Jerusalem was of the Jews. <div eID="gen30131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30132" type="x-p"/> Shall eat them as common things - By the law of Moses no man was permitted to eat of the fruit of his vineyard till the fifth year after planting. For the first three years it was considered uncircumcised, unclean, not fit to be eaten; in the fourth year it was holy to the Lord, the fruit belonged to Him; in the fifth year he might use it for himself, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23-Lev.19.25">Lev 19:23-25</reference>. But in the time here mentioned the fruit should be considered common - lawful at all times to be eaten.
entries.e314f6c9546bec4d300bc6d135089b5905381201: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30133" type="x-p"/> For there shall be a day - Literally, for this is the day, or the day is come. The watchmen - the prophets. <div eID="gen30133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30134" type="x-p"/> Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion - Let both Israelites and Jews join together in the worship of the Lord.
entries.374f14a23384dce3987c0e320fcc310a8492277e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30135" type="x-p"/> The chief of the nations - The same as Jacob or Israel; for most certainly this people was once the most honorable on the face of the earth. <div eID="gen30135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30136" type="x-p"/> O Lord, save thy people - Let the Jews earnestly intercede in behalf of their Israelitish brethren; or let them rejoice and praise the Lord, who hath saved the remnant of Israel. So Dr. Blayney thinks the clause should be understood.
entries.e1a613d8b1113ac30904cb3f6041d65dbdeae98e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30137" type="x-p"/> I will bring them from the north country - From Babylon. <div eID="gen30137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30138" type="x-p"/> From the coasts of the earth - The ten tribes were carried away partly into Assyria by Tiglath-pileser, and partly into Mesopotamia and Media by Shalmaneser, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Kgs 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>. Assyria and Media, being very distant from Palestine, might have been called, in prophetic language, the coasts of the earth. <div eID="gen30138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30139" type="x-p"/> The blind and the lame - I will so effectually remove all difficulties out of the way, so provide for them on the journey, so supernaturally support their bodies and minds, that the veriest invalids shall safely proceed to, and happily arrive at, the end of their journey.
entries.0c1ec9a0987a632ef7a2831ff5da60611868c0b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30140" type="x-p"/> They shall come with weeping - Duly penetrated with a sense of their sins, they shall deeply deplore them; and, while weeping for them, earnestly supplicate God to have mercy upon them. <div eID="gen30140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30141" type="x-p"/> By the rivers of waters - I will so guide and provide for them in the arid deserts, that they shall find streams of water whenever necessary. Every one knows of how much consequence water is to travelers in the eastern deserts. <div eID="gen30141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30142" type="x-p"/> Ephraim is my first-born - Ephraim, being the most considerable, is often put for the whole of the ten tribes.
entries.1cc486dfa43a704d48edf7e6b3580ecddc33bfa2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30143" type="x-p"/> And shall flow together - Perhaps this may refer to their assembling at the three great national feasts, the passover, pentecost, and tabernacles. <div eID="gen30143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30144" type="x-p"/> Their soul shall be as a watered garden - Full of the light, life, and power of God; so that they shall rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in every thing.
entries.fe9d06368b72a75a1bed840b569eb8203cb9f29a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen30144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30145" type="x-p"/> And I will satiate the soul of the priests - The worship of God being restored, they shall have their proper share of the victims brought to the temple.
entries.c41451871bdf6cfb882d0dd9653fb92aecf90471: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30146" type="x-p"/> A voice was heard in Ramah - The Ramah mentioned here, (for there were several towns of this name), was situated in the tribe of Benjamin, about six or seven miles from Jerusalem. Near this place Rachel was buried; who is here, in a beautiful figure of poetry, represented as coming out of her grave, and lamenting bitterly for the loss of her children, none of whom presented themselves to her view, all being slain or gone into exile. St. Matthew, who is ever fond of accommodation, applies these words, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.17">Mat 2:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.18">Mat 2:18</reference>, to the massacre of the children at Bethlehem. That is, they were suitable to that occasion, and therefore he so applied them; but they are not a prediction of that event.
entries.3e586ba9371b1401dc137f49484be740eda6eb23: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30147" type="x-p"/> They shall come again from the land of the enemy - This could not be said of the murdered innocents at Bethlehem; they never came again; but the Jews, who had gone into captivity, did come again from the land of their enemy to their own border.
entries.9d8841bc34593c4fc2483ec8a14b37100311b161: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30148" type="x-p"/> I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself - The exiled Israelites are in a state of deep repentance. <div eID="gen30148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30149" type="x-p"/> Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised - I was at first like an unbroken and untoward steer, the more I was chastised the more I rebelled; but now I have benefited by thy correction. <div eID="gen30149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30150" type="x-p"/> Turn thou me - I am now willing to take thy yoke upon me, but I have no power. I can only will and pray. Take the matter into thy own hand, and fully convert my soul.
entries.fd979d2aa4e768cea758a03bb0daaa9f246f92c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30151" type="x-p"/> After that I was turned - Converted from my sin, folly, and idolatry. <div eID="gen30151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30152" type="x-p"/> I repented - To conviction of sin, I now added contrition for sin. Conviction, in this sense of the word, must precede contrition or repentance. As soon as a man sees himself lost and undone, he is convicted of sin; when convicted, he begins to mourn. Thus contrition follows conviction. <div eID="gen30152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30153" type="x-p"/> I smote upon my thigh - My sorrow grew deeper and deeper; I smote upon my thigh through the extremity of my distress. This was a usual sign of deep affliction. See <reference osisRef="Eze.21.12">Eze 21:12</reference>. It was the same among the ancient Greeks. So Homer: - Ως εφατ' αυταρ Αρης θαλερω πεπληγετο μηρω Χερσι καταπρηνεσσ,ολοφυρομενος δε προσηυδα. <div eID="gen30153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30154" type="x-p"/> IL. lib. 15:113. "She spake: and with expanded arms, his thighs <div eID="gen30154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30155" type="x-p"/> Smiting, thus sorrowful, the god exclaimed." <div eID="gen30155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30156" type="x-p"/> Cowper. - αυταρ Αχιλλευς Μηρω πληξαμενος Πατροκληα προσεειπεν. <div eID="gen30156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30157" type="x-p"/> IL. lib. 16:124. "Achilles saw it, smote his thigh, and said." <div eID="gen30157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30158" type="x-p"/> Cowper. <div eID="gen30158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30159" type="x-p"/> I have often seen persons in deep grief act thus.
entries.dc48329cbc6ebee7c3d47373ba9eb0bc4339ad6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30160" type="x-p"/> Is Ephraim my dear son? - It is impossible to conceive any thing more tenderly affectionate than this. Let us consider the whole account. The ten tribes, called here Ephraim, for the reason before alleged, are represented as acknowledging their sins. I have heard Ephraim bemoaning himself; and in his lamentation he says, <div eID="gen30160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30161" type="x-p"/> 1. Thou hast chastised me. <div eID="gen30161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30162" type="x-p"/> 2. Though he at first rebelled against the chastisement, yet at last he submitted and acknowledged his offenses. <div eID="gen30162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30163" type="x-p"/> 3. He turned from all his offenses; he was converted. <div eID="gen30163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30164" type="x-p"/> 4. After his conversion, (שובי shubi), he repented; after conviction came contrition, as before stated. <div eID="gen30164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30165" type="x-p"/> 5. Being in a state of godly sorrow, he was instructed, הודעי hivvadei, he got a thorough knowledge of the desperate wickedness of his heart and life. <div eID="gen30165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30166" type="x-p"/> 6. Having received this instruction, he was filled with excessive grief; which is signified here by smiting on his thigh. See above. <div eID="gen30166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30167" type="x-p"/> 7. He finds that from his youth up he had been sinning against God; and although his youthful sins had long passed from his memory, yet the light of God brought them back, and he was ashamed and confounded at the sight of them. <div eID="gen30167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30168" type="x-p"/> 8. In this state of confusion and distress God sees him; and, commiserating his state, thus speaks: - <div eID="gen30168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30169" type="x-p"/> 1. Is Ephraim my dear son? Bad as he is in his own sight, and in the sight of my justice, he is now a penitent, and to me is precious. <div eID="gen30169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30170" type="x-p"/> 2. However loathsome and disfigured he may be with sin and sorrow, he is to me a pleasant child - a child of delights; one in whose conversion I delight, and my angels rejoice. <div eID="gen30170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30171" type="x-p"/> 3. I did speak against him: כי מדי דברי בו ki middey dabberi bo, for "from the abundance of my speaking in him;" accusing, threatening, promising, exhorting, encouraging; "I do still earnestly remember him." God has taken much pains with him, and is unwilling to give him up; but now that he repents, he has not received the grace of God utterly in vain. <div eID="gen30171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30172" type="x-p"/> 4. God feels a yearning desire towards him; המו מעי לו hamu meai lo, "my bowels are agitated for him." I feel nothing towards him but pity and love. When a sinner turns to God, God ceases to be angry with him. <div eID="gen30172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30173" type="x-p"/> 5. God expresses his determination to save him; ארחמנו רחם rachem arachamennu, "I will be affectionately merciful to him, with tender mercy, saith the Lord." He shall find that I treat him as a father does a returning prodigal son. So every penitent is sure to find mercy at the hand of God.
entries.c13b5c9741d2943ba4af63f285186e5dedd4be8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30174" type="x-p"/> Set thee up waymarks - Alluding to stones, or heaps of stones, which travelers in the desert set up to ascertain the way, that they may know how to return. Mark the way to Babylon: thither ye shall certainly go; but from it ye shall as certainly return.
entries.0c39ca26b01bf45f4331990d8798df4097fc974c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30175" type="x-p"/> A woman shall compass a man - נקבה תסובב גבר nekebah tesobeb gaber, "A weak woman shall compass or circumvent a strong man." This place has given much trouble to Biblical critics. By many Christian writers it is considered a prophecy of the miraculous conception of the holy virgin; but as I am sure no such meaning is in the words, nor in the context, so I am satisfied no such meaning can be fairly brought out of them. Houbigant thinks there is a small error in the text, i.e., תשובב teshobeb, shall return, and not תסובב tesobeb, shall compass. This reading is found in two of Kennicott's MSS., and he contends that the passage should be read, "The wife shall return to her husband;" alluding to the conversion of the Jewish people, called above a backsliding daughter. This makes a good sense; but I do not see why this should be called a new thing in the earth. After all, I think it likely that the Jews in their present distressed circumstances are represented under the similitude of a weak defenseless female נקבה nekebah; and the Chaldeans under that of a fierce strong man, גבר gaber, who had prevailed over and oppressed this weak woman. But, notwithstanding the disparity between them, God would cause the woman - the weak defenseless Jews, to compass - to overcome, the strong man - the powerful Babylonians. And this the prophet says would be a new thing in the land; for in such a case the lame would take the prey. The context favors both these meanings. Dr. Blayney gives a sense very near to this: "A weak woman shall repulse a strong or mighty man." It is most likely a proverbial expression.
entries.a9a07f969abc508d2158cc9408142f37c460435a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30176" type="x-p"/> The Lord bless thee, O habitation of justice - After their return they shall De remarkably prosperous. Piety and industry shall go hand in hand; they shall have their husbandmen, their shepherds, and neatherds, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.24">Jer 31:24</reference>. And Jerusalem shall become a righteous city, and the temple shall be a place of holiness; so the weary there shall have rest, and the sorrowful shall be abundantly comforted, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.24">Jer 31:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.25">Jer 31:25</reference>.
entries.822d83c0ed07c54546499f3db701f06a21c2c4ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen30176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30177" type="x-p"/> Upon this I awaked - It appears that the prophecy, commencing with <reference osisRef="Jer.30.2">Jer 30:2</reference> and ending with <reference osisRef="Jer.31.25">Jer 31:25</reference> of this chapter, was delivered to the prophet in a dream. Dahler supposes it to be a wish; that the prophet, though he could not hope to live to that time, might be permitted to awake up from his tomb; and, having seen this prosperity, would be content to return to his grave.
entries.b2a78a6e5e4f0e55740e8e8f45b38ed472c4aa04: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen30177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30178" type="x-p"/> I will sow - with the seed of man and with the seed of beast - I will multiply both men and cattle.
entries.4a04ad3dde837542c4a0edfafa5c7a75feb2520f: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen30178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30179" type="x-p"/> The fathers have eaten a sour grape - A proverbial expression for, "The children suffer for the offenses of their parents." This is explained in the next verse: "Every one shall die for his own iniquity." No child shall suffer Divine punition for the sin of his father; only so far as he acts in the same way can he be said to bear the sins of his parents.
entries.fec7585d2538004a5655b0f5022b6d707ede1786: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen30179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30180" type="x-p"/> A new covenant - The Christian dispensation.
entries.1e2743c15d31ce52fa3e565bd40052246d831ca8: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen30180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30181" type="x-p"/> After those days - When vision and prophecy shall be sealed up, and Jesus have assumed that body which was prepared for him, and have laid down his life for the redemption of a lost world, and, having ascended on high, shall have obtained the gift of the Holy Spirit to purify the heart; then God's law shall, by it, be put in their inward parts, and written on their hearts; so that all within and all without shall be holiness to the Lord. Then God will be truly their God, received and acknowledged as their portion, and the sole object of their devotion; and they shall be his people, filled with holiness, and made partakers of the Divine nature, so that they shall perfectly love him and worthily magnify his name.
entries.6609d514d12c03cc2cecfb0cdab7adc46239acb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen30181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30182" type="x-p"/> And they shall teach no more - It shall be a time of universal light and knowledge; all shall know God in Christ, from the least to the greatest; the children shall be taught to read the New Covenant, and to understand the terms of their salvation. <div eID="gen30182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30183" type="x-p"/> I will forgive their iniquity - It shall be a time of General Pardon; multitudes shall be daily in the Christian Church receiving the witness of God's Spirit, and in their life and conversation witnessing a good confession. How wonderfully is this prophecy fulfilled in the age of Bibles, Sunday schools, and village preaching.
